svg.title: Three quality indicators for a first bladder tumour resection, when to resect again, and the unsettled question of blue light
svg.desc: Schematic: three quality indicators for a first transurethral resection of a bladder tumour, when a second resection is indicated, and why blue light remains unsettled. Across the top are three cards holding the three checkable quality indicators. The first is whether there is detrusor muscle in the specimen: the guideline states that the absence of detrusor muscle is associated with a significantly higher risk of residual disease, early recurrence and tumour under-staging, and that its presence is considered a surrogate criterion of resection quality and is required, except in Ta low-grade / G1 tumours. The second is whether the resection was visibly complete: an incomplete initial resection, or doubt about completeness, is itself the first indication for doing it again, and if the report does not record whether the resection was visibly complete, that is a question to put. The third is whether the specimens were submitted separately labelled: specimens from different biopsies and resection fractions go to the pathologist in separately labelled containers, the tumour base is submitted separately, especially for large or multifocal tumours or where en-bloc resection is not feasible, and cauterisation is avoided as far as possible. Next come the numbers for the detrusor cell: recurrence at the first follow-up cystoscopy was 44.4 per cent where the specimen contained no muscle and 21.7 per cent where it did, and 67.7 per cent of specimens in the same cohort contained detrusor muscle. The population label gives a prospective Edinburgh cohort, n=356, of newly diagnosed patients whose resection was judged visibly complete at operation; the odds ratio is 2.9 (95 per cent confidence interval 1.6 to 5.4), P=0.0002; and a note adds that an odds ratio is a ratio of odds between two groups rather than a multiple of the probability, that both absolute numbers are given, and that the absolute numbers are what to read. The following panel is quality measured twice, in two columns. On the left, the Scottish national quality indicator programme: five-year recurrence was 38.9 per cent in hospitals meeting the detrusor sampling benchmark against 44.3 per cent in the rest, 5.4 percentage points lower (95 per cent confidence interval 1.6 to 9.2), P=0.005; the multivariable hazard ratio was 0.81 (0.73 to 0.91) and the progression-free survival hazard ratio 0.62 (0.45 to 0.84); the population was 2,688 patients with non-muscle-invasive disease among 3,899 newly diagnosed between April 2014 and March 2017, with a median follow-up of 60.3 months, and the programme had no national pre-implementation control group, making this an observational association. On the right, checklists against seniority, two datasets pointing opposite ways: the Edinburgh series found senior surgeons' specimens more often contained detrusor muscle, while a prospective collaborative database of 503 cases - 265 senior consultants, 149 junior consultants, 89 residents - found the opposite, residents' specimens containing detrusor muscle more often, odds ratio 1.75 (1.03 to 2.99), P=0.04; residents and junior consultants completed the surgical checklist more often, 56 per cent and 56 per cent against 44 per cent, P=0.009; and five-year recurrence-free survival was unrelated to seniority. Below the two columns a line records that what can be read out of this is that the checklist explains the difference better than seniority does, not that anyone resects better, and that the figure draws no ranking by seniority. The next panel is the second resection: three indications - an incomplete initial resection or doubt about completeness, no detrusor muscle in the initial specimen, and T1 tumours - two clearly marked exceptions, Ta low grade / G1 and primary CIS, and the timing, within two to six weeks of the initial resection and including the original tumour site, with retrospective data showing that resections done at 14 to 42 days gave better recurrence-free and progression-free survival than those at 43 to 90 days. Then what a second resection actually finds. Four bars come from a meta-analysis in T1 disease (29 studies; 3,566 patients for residual disease and 2,556 for upstaging): residual tumour in all patients 0.56 (95 per cent confidence interval 0.48 to 0.63); upstaging to muscle invasion in all patients 0.10 (0.06 to 0.14); residual tumour 0.47 in the 1,565 whose first specimen already contained muscle; and upstaging still 0.10 in that subgroup, marked as no lower. A line is picked out beside them: "there was muscle this time" does not mean "no second resection is needed". Below, a second systematic review (31 studies, 8,409 patients with high-grade Ta and T1 disease) gives ranges: residual tumour 17 to 67 per cent for Ta and 20 to 71 per cent for T1, with most residual disease, 36 to 86 per cent, at the original resection site; upstaging from Ta to T1 or above 0 to 8 per cent, and from T1 to T2 or above 0 to 32 per cent. Contemporary numbers are lower: in an updated meta-analysis of 81 studies, T1 patients treated by conventional resection in the 2010s had any residual disease in 31.4 per cent (26.0 to 37.2) and upstaging in 2.8 per cent (2.0 to 3.8), with a warning of potential publication bias. The size of the benefit is set down honestly: after adjustment, recurrence-free survival hazard ratio 0.78 (0.62 to 0.97) and overall survival 0.86 (0.81 to 0.93) were better, but progression-free survival 0.74 (0.47 to 1.15) and cancer-specific survival 0.94 (0.86 to 1.03) showed no difference. The panel closes with the guideline's counter-example: in one single-centre series 104 of 209 patients with high-grade Ta disease had a second resection and only 1 was upstaged to T1, none to T2 or above, while the patients for whom the guideline indicated a second resection had significantly worse recurrence-free and progression-free survival - the shape of selection bias. The next panel is en-bloc resection: the phase 3 randomised trial that met its primary endpoint (multicentre, Hong Kong; 350 randomised, 276 pathologically confirmed non-muscle-invasive, tumours 3 cm or less) gave one-year recurrence of 29 per cent (95 per cent confidence interval 18 to 37) against 38 per cent (28 to 46) for standard resection, P=0.007; one-year progression 0 per cent against 2.6 per cent (0 to 5.5), P=0.065; detrusor sampling and the other secondary endpoints similar in the two arms; and median operating time 28 against 22 minutes. A note records that two further randomised trials found no difference in time to recurrence, so what can be said is that at 3 cm or less, with one-year recurrence as the endpoint, one trial saw a difference - not that en-bloc resection is better - and that this figure draws no ranking of techniques. The penultimate panel is blue light, carrying a red status pill reading "unsettled", in two columns with "seeing more clearly is not the same as recurring less" between them and no arrow. On the left, detection: patient-level sensitivity 92 per cent for blue light against 71 per cent for white light, biopsy-level 93 per cent against 65 per cent, at the cost of lower specificity, 63 per cent against 81 per cent, with inflammation, a recent resection and the three months after BCG instillation all capable of causing false positives. On the right, recurrence: in the PHOTO randomised trial the three-year recurrence hazard ratio was 0.94 (0.69 to 1.28), P=0.70; the three-year recurrence-free rate 57.8 per cent against 61.6 per cent; and the cost £876 more over three years with no difference in quality-adjusted life years; the population was 22 hospitals in the United Kingdom, 538 randomised and 426 in the primary analysis, in newly diagnosed intermediate and high-risk non-muscle-invasive disease. A footnote records that the two randomised trials of narrow-band imaging were also negative overall with a signal only in a low-risk subgroup, and that the guideline goes no further than a weak recommendation - use methods to improve tumour visualisation during resection, if available - while writing that further investigation is needed. The last panel lists the seven lines that should appear on the pathology report: tumour location, grade, stage, lymphovascular invasion, subtypes of urothelial carcinoma, presence of CIS and detrusor muscle; with a small box beside it noting that where cytology is positive but cystoscopy shows nothing, the guideline asks that upper tract urothelial carcinoma, CIS in the bladder and tumour in the prostatic urethra all be excluded. At the foot of the figure is the Taiwanese section: the fee schedule lists 78008C, endoscopic resection of a bladder tumour including cystoscopy, at 8,027 points, the first note reading that a cystoscopy report must accompany the claim; bladder instillation is 50011C at 260 points; of the 3,809 bladder cancers in the Taiwan Cancer Registry long-form report for 2023, 1,630 (42.79 per cent) had resection combined with intravesical chemotherapy and 558 (14.65 per cent) resection alone; a full-text search for "blue light", "photodynamic", "narrow-band imaging" and "en-bloc resection" returns nothing, so the billing office or case manager has to be asked and nothing is inferred either way; and whether Taiwan has surgical quality indicators of the Scottish kind, or how often second resections are done, cannot be established from official statistics.

g.text: THREE QUALITY INDICATORS, AND WHEN A
SECOND RESECTION IS INDICATED
Three quality indicators
for a first resection, and
when it has to be done
again
This operation is treatment, specimen collection and
the foundation of every later decision all at once:
whether anything is instilled, whether a second
resection is needed, whether the stage can be
believed, all rest on how this one went.
So the question on this figure is not whether it "went
well" but three things that can be checked. There is no
ranking of surgeons by seniority here, and no arrow
from blue light to fewer recurrences - that cell is
unsettled.
Three quality indicators that can be
checked
1 | Is there detrusor muscle in the specimen
The guideline sentence: the absence of detrusor muscle in the
specimen is associated with a significantly higher risk of residual
disease, early recurrence and tumour under-staging.
The presence of detrusor muscle is considered a surrogate
criterion of the resection quality, and it is required, except in Ta
low-grade / G1 tumours.
2 | Was the resection visibly complete
An incomplete initial resection, or doubt about its completeness, is
itself the first indication for doing it again.
If the report does not record whether the resection was visibly
complete, that is a question to put.
3 | Were the specimens submitted separately labelled
Specimens from different biopsies and resection fractions must
be referred to the pathologist in separately labelled containers.
The tumour base is submitted separately, especially for large or
multifocal tumours, or where en-bloc resection is not feasible.
And cauterisation is avoided as far as possible, so the tissue is
not damaged.
The detrusor cell has been measured
Recurrence at the first follow-up cystoscopy
No muscle in the specimen
Muscle in the specimen
In the same cohort, 67.7% of specimens contained detrusor
muscle.
Prospective Edinburgh cohort, n=356, of newly diagnosed patients in whom
the resection was judged visibly complete at operation. Odds ratio 2.9 (95%
confidence interval 1.6-5.4), P=0.0002. An odds ratio is a ratio of odds
between two groups, not a multiple of the probability; both absolute
numbers are given here, and the absolute numbers are what to read. The
authors note that the association holds for small, low-grade tumours as
well.
Quality is not an abstract adjective; it has
been measured twice
The Scottish national quality indicator programme
Five-year recurrence
38.9% in hospitals meeting the detrusor sampling benchmark, 44.3%
in the rest
The gap
5.4 percentage points lower (95% confidence interval 1.6-9.2),
Multivariable hazard ratio
Progression-free survival hazard ratio
3,899 people newly diagnosed with bladder cancer between April 2014 and
March 2017, of whom 2,688 had non-muscle-invasive disease, with a
median follow-up of 60.3 months. The authors state that the programme
had no national pre-implementation control group, so this is an
observational association and not a randomised comparison.
Checklists against seniority: two datasets pointing opposite
ways
The Edinburgh series found that senior surgeons' specimens
more often contained detrusor muscle.
A prospective collaborative database of 503 cases (265 senior
consultants, 149 junior consultants, 89 residents) pointed the
other way: residents' specimens contained detrusor muscle
more often (odds ratio 1.75, 1.03-2.99, P=0.04).
Residents and junior consultants completed the surgical
checklist more often: 56% and 56% against 44%, P=0.009.
Five-year recurrence-free survival was unrelated to the
operator's seniority.
What can be read out of this is that the checklist explains the difference
better than seniority does, not that anyone resects better - this figure
draws no ranking by seniority
"I got it all out" and "I finished the
resection" are two different sentences
Three situations in which a second resection is indicated (a
strong recommendation)
After an incomplete initial resection, or where there is doubt
about its completeness.
If there is no detrusor muscle in the initial specimen.
In T1 tumours.
Two exceptions, to be remembered alongside them
Ta low grade / G1.
Primary CIS.
Otherwise the rule turns into "no muscle means another resection,
always".
Timing (a weaker recommendation, but a specific one)
Within two to six weeks of the initial resection, and this second
resection should include the original tumour site.
Retrospective data show that resections done at 14 to 42 days
gave better recurrence-free and progression-free survival
than those done at 43 to 90 days. Doing it again is not a
comment on the first operation; it is one of the standard steps
in this disease.
What a second resection actually finds
Meta-analysis in T1 disease (29 studies; 3,566 patients for
residual disease, 2,556 for upstaging)
Residual tumour, all patients
95% confidence interval 0.48-0.63
Upstaging to muscle invasion, all patients
Residual tumour, the 1,565 whose first specimen had muscle
subgroup
Upstaging, the 1,565 whose first specimen had muscle
subgroup, no lower
That line is worth reading twice: "there was muscle this time"
does not mean "no second resection is needed".
A second systematic review (31 studies, 8,409 patients with
high-grade Ta and T1 disease) gives ranges, which show
how far the studies differ
Residual tumour
17 to 67% for Ta and 20 to 71% for T1; most residual disease, 36 to
86%, sits at the original resection site
Upstaging
Ta to T1 or above, 0 to 8%; T1 to T2 or above, 0 to 32%
Contemporary numbers are lower: in an updated meta-analysis of
81 studies, T1 patients treated by conventional resection in the
2010s had any residual disease in 31.4% (26.0-37.2) and upstaging in
2.8% (2.0-3.8) at second resection - though the authors warn of
potential publication bias.
How large the benefit is has to be stated honestly too (same
meta-analysis, after adjustment for confounding)
Recurrence-free survival
hazard ratio 0.78 (0.62-0.97): better
Overall survival
Progression-free survival
0.74 (0.47-1.15): no difference
Cancer-specific survival
0.94 (0.86-1.03): no difference
The guideline adds a counter-example of its own: in one single-centre
series, 104 of 209 patients with high-grade Ta disease had a second
resection, and only 1 was upstaged to T1 with none to T2 or above; while
the patients for whom the guideline indicated a second resection had
significantly worse recurrence-free and progression-free survival. That
is not the harm of a second resection; it is that the people selected for one
were at higher risk to begin with - which is what selection bias looks like.
En-bloc resection: one trial finds a
difference, two do not
The phase 3 randomised trial that met its primary endpoint
(multicentre, Hong Kong; 350 randomised, 276 pathologically
confirmed non-muscle-invasive, tumours 3 cm or less)
One-year recurrence: en-bloc resection
95% confidence interval 18-37
One-year recurrence: standard resection
P value
One-year progression
Detrusor sampling and the other secondary endpoints
similar in the two arms
Median operating time
28 against 22 minutes
Two further randomised trials found no difference in time to recurrence.
So what can be said is that "at 3 cm or less, with one-year recurrence as
the endpoint, one trial saw a difference" - not that en-bloc resection is
better. This figure draws no ranking of techniques.
Blue light sees more clearly; whether it
means fewer recurrences is unsettled
Unsettled
Detection: photodynamic diagnosis (blue light) against white
light
Patient-level sensitivity: blue light
Patient-level sensitivity: white light
Biopsy-level sensitivity: blue light
Biopsy-level sensitivity: white light
The cost is lower specificity: 63% for blue light against 81% for
white light. Inflammation, a recent resection and the three months
after BCG instillation can all cause false positives.
No arrow between these
Recurrence: the PHOTO randomised trial
Three-year recurrence hazard ratio
Three-year recurrence-free rate
57.8% against 61.6%
Cost
£876 more over three years, with no difference in quality-adjusted
life years
22 hospitals in the United Kingdom, 538 randomised (426 in the primary
analysis), in newly diagnosed intermediate and high-risk
non-muscle-invasive disease.
Seeing more clearly is not the same as recurring less (no
arrow between these two columns)
The two randomised trials of narrow-band imaging were also
negative overall, with a signal only in a low-risk subgroup. The
guideline goes no further than a weak recommendation - "use
methods to improve tumour visualisation during TURBT, if
available" - and writes that further investigation is needed. This
cell has no settled answer today, not every hospital can offer it,
and it is a question for your own consultant.
Which lines should appear on the pathology
report
The seven items the guideline asks for
Tumour location
Grade
Stage
Lymphovascular invasion
Subtypes of urothelial carcinoma
Presence of CIS
Detrusor muscle
Those seven are the checklist to go through when the report
arrives. The cell left blank, and the cell that says "none", are what
the next clinic appointment is really about.
And one particular situation: positive cytology with a normal
cystoscopy
The guideline asks that upper tract urothelial carcinoma, CIS
in the bladder (by mapping biopsies or blue-light guided
biopsies) and tumour in the prostatic urethra all be excluded.
In Taiwan: what can be looked up, and what cannot
The fee schedule lists 78008C, endoscopic resection of a
bladder tumour including cystoscopy, at 8,027 points, with the
first note reading, word for word, that a cystoscopy report
must accompany the claim.
Bladder instillation is 50011C, 260 points.
Of the 3,809 bladder cancers in the Taiwan Cancer Registry
long-form report for 2023, 1,630 (42.79%) had resection
combined with intravesical chemotherapy and 558 (14.65%)
resection alone.
A full-text search of the fee schedule for "blue light",
"photodynamic", "narrow-band imaging" and "en-bloc
resection" returns nothing at all - there is no line item to find, so
whether anything is payable has to be asked of the billing office
or your case manager. Nothing is inferred either way.
Whether Taiwan has surgical quality indicators of the Scottish
kind, and how often second resections are done, cannot be
established from official statistics.
Schematic, redrawn from the EAU 2026 guideline on
non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer, Mariappan 2010 and 2024, Del
Giudice 2023, Naselli 2018, Cumberbatch 2018, Yanagisawa 2024,
Teoh 2024, Heer 2022 (PHOTO), the Taiwanese National Health
Insurance fee schedule and the Taiwan Cancer Registry long-form
report for 2023; not reproduced from the figures of the original
papers. The cohorts, designs and endpoints of the underlying studies
differ, so the data points must not be compared directly.
